title: Heart rate: the climb, the ceiling and the slow athlete's heart
goal: Explain how heart rate rises with work, how well age formulas predict HRmax, why training barely changes HRmax, and the debate over why athletes' resting heart rate is low.

steps.title: Heart rate climbs with the work
steps.text:
You've met the two controls in the nervous system module: the [vagal brake](g:vagal-tone) and the [sympathetic](g:sympathetic) accelerator. From rest to maximal exercise the balance shifts step by step, from about 4 : 1 vagal to about 4 : 1 sympathetic [[c:hr-balance]]. The vagus never fully switches off.

The result is a heart rate that climbs with the workload. Above rest it tracks oxygen uptake closely: the share of your [heart-rate reserve](g:heart-rate-reserve) you use matches the share of your VO₂ reserve (VO₂max − resting VO₂), not the share of VO₂max [[c:hr-hrr-vo2r]].

**%HRR = (HR − HRrest) ÷ (HRmax − HRrest)**

That is why HR works as an intensity gauge, as long as you know your real HRmax and resting HR.

claims.text: From rest to maximal exercise, autonomic control of HR shifts from about 4 : 1 vagal to about 4 : 1 sympathetic, with the vagus active throughout.

evidence.quote: Results indicate that the PSNS remains functionally active throughout exercise and that increases in HR from rest to maximal exercise result from an increasing workload-related transition from a 4 : 1 vagal-sympathetic balance to a 4 : 1 sympatho-vagal balance.

claims.text: Percentage of heart-rate reserve matches percentage of VO₂ reserve, not percentage of VO₂max.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, %HRR should not be considered equivalent to %VO2max. Rather, %HRR is equivalent to %VO2R, and this relationship should be used in exercise prescription.

steps.title: What share of the reserve?
steps.problem: A cyclist rests at 50 beats·min⁻¹ and has a measured HRmax of 190. On a climb his HR is 155. What percentage of his heart-rate reserve is he using?
steps: %HRR = 105 ÷ 140 = 0.75, so 75%, which is about 75% of his VO₂ reserve.
Compare: 155 ÷ 190 = 82% of HRmax. %HRmax and %HRR are different scales; don't mix them.

steps.title: HRmax and the age formulas
steps.text:
[HRmax](g:hrmax) falls with age. The old rule, 220 − age, had never been checked in enough older adults. A meta-analysis of 18,712 people, then a lab study of 514, found [[c:hr-tanaka]]:

**HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age**

It held for men and women and at all activity levels; 220 − age underestimates HRmax in older people.

But a formula predicts the average, not you. In 762 adults, the standard error of the prediction was about **11 beats·min⁻¹** for Tanaka and 12 for 220 − age [[c:hr-formula-error]]. Roughly one person in three misses by more than 11, and one in twenty by more than 22.

Measure HRmax in a maximal test or hard race when you can [[c:hr-measure]].

claims.text: The 220 − age rule had not been tested in enough older adults. In a meta-analysis of 18,712 people, HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age, independent of sex and activity level; 220 − age underestimates it in older adults.

evidence.quote: Despite its importance and widespread use, the validity of the HRmax equation has never been established in a sample that included a sufficient number of older adults.
First, a meta-analytic approach was used to collect group mean HRmax values from 351 studies involving 492 groups and 18,712 subjects.

2) HRmax is predicted, to a large extent, by age alone and is independent of gender and habitual physical activity status. Our findings suggest that the currently used equation underestimates HRmax in older adults.

claims.text: Age formulas predict an individual's HRmax with a standard error of about 11–12 beats·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: The standard error of estimate (SEE) of predicted HRmax was 12.4 and 11.4 bpm for the Fox and Tanaka formulas, respectively, indicating a wide-spread of measured-HRmax values are compared to their age-predicted values.
Bland-Altman plots revealed wide limits of agreement for all nine APMHR equations, suggesting poor agreement between measured and predicted

claims.text: Where possible, HRmax should be measured in a maximal test rather than predicted.

evidence.quote: Individuals should use data from GXTs to determine HRmax when applicable to ensure accuracy.

steps.title: Predicting HRmax, and its error
steps.problem: Predict HRmax for a 45-year-old triathlete with both formulas, and give the range two in three people of that age would fall into.
steps: Tanaka: 0.7 × 45 = 31.5, so 208 − 31.5 = 176.5, about 177 beats·min⁻¹. Multiply first, then subtract.
With a standard error of about 11, two in three 45-year-olds fall between about 166 and 188. The two formulas differ by 2 beats; the person-to-person spread is ten times bigger.

steps.title: Training barely moves HRmax
steps.text:
The usual view is that HRmax is relatively unchanged by training. A review argues it can still shift by **3–7%**: down a little with training, up a little with detraining or a taper [[c:hr-max-training]].

Below max, the change is large. At the same absolute power or pace, trained people's HR is lower [[c:hr-submax-lower]]. Their SV is bigger, so the same Q needs fewer beats, and sympathetic drive to the heart is lower.

So HR at a fixed power or pace falling over a training block is a sign of fitness. A slightly lower HRmax after a big block isn't a loss of fitness, and zones built on an old HRmax may need checking.

claims.text: HRmax is generally considered relatively unaltered by training; a review estimates it can change by 3–7%, falling with training and rising with tapering or detraining.

evidence.quote: While it is known that aerobic training decreases submaximal HR (HRsubmax) at a given absolute exercise workload, the general consensus is that maximum HR (HRmax) is relatively unaltered regardless of training status in a given population.
Therefore, analysis reveals that HRmax can be altered by 3 to 7% with aerobic training/detraining.
Furthermore, evidence suggests that tapering/detraining can increase HRmax.

claims.text: Endurance training lowers HR at a given submaximal workload, partly by reducing sympathetic activity to the heart.

evidence.quote: Long-term endurance training also decreases submaximal exercise heart rate by reducing sympathetic activity to the heart.

steps.title: The athlete's slow resting heart
steps.text:
Endurance athletes often have a slow resting HR: [sinus bradycardia](g:sinus-bradycardia) [[c:hr-brady-common]]. Why?

**A stronger vagal brake.** The classic answer: training raises parasympathetic and lowers sympathetic activity at rest, perhaps with a lower intrinsic rate as well [[c:hr-brady-vagal]].

**A slower pacemaker.** With both branches blocked by drugs, world-class oarsmen still had a lower [intrinsic heart rate](g:intrinsic-heart-rate) than non-athletes, 81 against 102 beats·min⁻¹. The authors put the oarsmen's slow resting HR down to the [sinoatrial node](g:sa-node-pacemaker) alone [[c:hr-katona]]. In trained mice the slow rate persisted after blockade, with less of the HCN4 'funny' ion channel in the node [[c:hr-dsouza]].

The human studies are few and small; the most direct work is in mice.

claims.text: Endurance athletes have sinus bradycardia, a slow resting heart rate.

evidence.quote: Endurance athletes exhibit sinus bradycardia, that is a slow resting heart rate, associated with a higher incidence of sinus node (pacemaker) disease and electronic pacemaker implantation.

claims.text: Endurance training raises parasympathetic and lowers sympathetic activity at rest, which, with a possible fall in intrinsic HR, lowers resting HR.

evidence.quote: Endurance training increases parasympathetic activity and decreases sympathetic activity in the human heart at rest. These two training-induced autonomic effects, coupled with a possible reduction in intrinsic heart rate, decrease resting heart rate.

claims.text: Under full autonomic blockade, world-class oarsmen had an intrinsic HR of 81 against 102 beats·min⁻¹ in non-athletes; the authors attributed their low resting HR solely to the lower intrinsic rate.

evidence.quote: In athletes the control heart rate [55 +/- 3.3 (SD) beats/min] and R0 (81 +/- 8.3 beats/min) were lower than in nonathletes (62 +/- 6.0, P less than 0.01 and 102 +/- 11, P less than 0.001, respectively).
the lower resting heart rate in oarsmen is solely due to a reduction in intrinsic cardiac rate, and not to an increase in parasympathetic tone.

claims.text: In mice, training bradycardia persisted after autonomic blockade and was caused by remodelling of the sinus node, including less HCN4.

evidence.quote: Here we show that training-induced bradycardia is not a consequence of changes in the activity of the autonomic nervous system but is caused by intrinsic electrophysiological changes in the sinus node.
We demonstrate that training-induced bradycardia persists after blockade of the autonomous nervous system in vivo in mice and in vitro in the denervated sinus node.
We also show that a widespread remodelling of pacemaker ion channels, notably a downregulation of HCN4 and the corresponding ionic current, If.

debate.question: Is athletes' slow resting heart rate mainly a stronger vagal brake or a slower sinoatrial node?

sides.position: Mainly autonomic: training raises vagal and lowers sympathetic activity to the heart at rest.
Mainly intrinsic: the sinoatrial node itself is remodelled and fires more slowly, even with the nerves blocked.

points: HR climbs with workload as control shifts from about 4 : 1 vagal to 4 : 1 sympathetic; %HRR matches %VO₂ reserve.
HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age on average, but the error for one person is about 11 beats·min⁻¹: measure it when you can.
Training barely moves HRmax (a few per cent, usually down) but clearly lowers HR at a given power or pace.
Athletes' resting bradycardia: classically a stronger vagal brake; blockade studies and mouse work point to a slower sinoatrial node. Still debated.

variants.stem: A runner rests at 48 beats·min⁻¹ and has a measured HRmax of 188. During a tempo run her HR is 153. What percentage of her heart-rate reserve is she using?

options.why: That is %HRmax (153 ÷ 188), a different scale from %HRR.
This divides by HRmax (105 ÷ 188) instead of by the reserve, HRmax − HRrest.
This divides by the current HR (105 ÷ 153) instead of by the reserve.

variants.stem: A cyclist rests at 55 beats·min⁻¹ and has a measured HRmax of 185. On an endurance ride his HR is 120. What percentage of his heart-rate reserve is he using?

options.why: That is %HRmax (120 ÷ 185), a different scale from %HRR.
This divides by HRmax (65 ÷ 185) instead of by the reserve, HRmax − HRrest.
This divides by the current HR (65 ÷ 120) instead of by the reserve.

variants.stem: A triathlete rests at 42 beats·min⁻¹ and has a measured HRmax of 182. On the run leg her HR is 133. What percentage of her heart-rate reserve is she using?

options.why: That is %HRmax (133 ÷ 182), a different scale from %HRR.
This divides by HRmax (91 ÷ 182) instead of by the reserve, HRmax − HRrest.
This divides by the current HR (91 ÷ 133) instead of by the reserve.

variants.stem: A cyclist reaches maximal effort at the end of a ramp test. What is the state of the vagal brake on his heart?

options.text: Still active, but outweighed about 4 : 1 by sympathetic drive
options.why: Right: the vagus stays functionally active throughout exercise; the balance shifts to about 4 : 1 sympathetic at max.

options.text: Fully switched off from the first minute of exercise
options.why: That is the older model; the review finds vagal activity active all the way to max.

options.text: Stronger than at rest, to protect the heart
options.why: Vagal influence falls as the work rises; at rest it is dominant, about 4 : 1.

options.text: Replaced by the baroreflex, which sets HR alone
options.why: The baroreflex works through the vagal and sympathetic nerves; it doesn't replace them.

variants.stem: Using HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × age, what is the predicted HRmax of a 50-year-old cyclist?

options.text: 173 beats·min⁻¹
170 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: That is 220 − age, the older rule, not the formula given.

options.text: 157 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This subtracts 0.7 and 50 separately (208 − 0.7 − 50). Multiply 0.7 × age first.

options.text: 243 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds 0.7 × age instead of subtracting it.

variants.solution: HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × 50 = 208 − 35 = 173 beats·min⁻¹ (with an error of about ±11 for one person).

options.text: 187 beats·min⁻¹
190 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: That is 220 − age, the older rule, not the formula given.

options.text: 177 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This subtracts 0.7 and 30 separately (208 − 0.7 − 30). Multiply 0.7 × age first.

options.text: 229 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds 0.7 × age instead of subtracting it.

variants.solution: HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × 30 = 208 − 21 = 187 beats·min⁻¹ (with an error of about ±11 for one person).

options.text: 163 beats·min⁻¹
156 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: That is 220 − age, the older rule, which underestimates HRmax in older people.

options.text: 143 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This subtracts 0.7 and 64 separately (208 − 0.7 − 64). Multiply 0.7 × age first.

options.text: 253 beats·min⁻¹

variants.solution: HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × 64 = 208 − 44.8 = 163.2 ≈ 163 beats·min⁻¹ (with an error of about ±11 for one person).

variants.stem: A 40-year-old runner set her zones from 208 − 0.7 × age = 180 beats·min⁻¹. In a 10 km race her HR sits at 186 for the last 15 minutes, and she feels fine afterwards. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Her true HRmax is above the formula's estimate
options.why: Right: a formula typically misses one person's HRmax by about 11 beats·min⁻¹. Holding 186 means her HRmax is higher; her zones need resetting.

options.text: Her heart worked dangerously above its maximum
options.why: Nobody can exceed their own HRmax; it was the estimate that was wrong, not her heart.

options.text: Her watch must have been misreading
options.why: Possible, but a steady, plausible reading fits the known size of formula error far better.

options.text: She ran the whole time above her VO₂max
options.why: No one can hold above VO₂max for 15 minutes; and her max was simply underestimated.

variants.stem: After three months of base training, a cyclist's heart rate at 200 W has dropped from 150 to 138 beats·min⁻¹. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A bigger stroke volume, so the same Q needs fewer beats
options.why: Right: Q at 200 W stays about the same; with a bigger SV and less sympathetic drive, HR is lower.

options.text: His HRmax fell by the same 12 beats
options.why: HRmax changes only a few per cent with training, and it doesn't set HR at a submaximal power.

options.text: His heart got weaker and can't speed up
options.why: A weaker heart would need more beats for the same Q, not fewer.

options.text: His cardiac output at 200 W fell by half
options.why: The muscles need about the same O₂ at 200 W, so Q stays similar; what changes is how it is made.

variants.stem: According to a review of training studies, by how much can endurance training change HRmax?

options.text: A few per cent, usually down
options.why: Right: the review estimates 3–7%, falling with training and rising with detraining or a taper.

options.text: Not at all, in anyone
options.why: Too strong: the general view is 'relatively unaltered', but studies report shifts of 3–7%.

options.text: Up by 10–20%
options.why: HRmax doesn't rise with training; if anything it falls slightly.

options.text: Down by about a third
options.why: Far beyond the 3–7% the review found.

variants.stem: With both autonomic branches blocked by drugs, a group of world-class rowers have a heart rate of 81 beats·min⁻¹ and a group of non-athletes 102. What does this most directly suggest?

options.text: The rowers' sinoatrial node fires more slowly by itself
options.why: Right: with the nerves blocked, what is left is the node's intrinsic rate, and it is lower in the rowers.

options.text: The rowers have a stronger vagal brake
options.why: The blockade removed the vagal brake, yet the gap remained, so this gap can't be vagal.

options.text: The rowers have more sympathetic drive
options.why: Sympathetic effects were blocked too, and more sympathetic drive would raise HR, not lower it.

options.text: The rowers breathe more slowly at rest
options.why: Breathing affects HR through the vagus, which was blocked; it can't explain a gap under full blockade.

variants.stem: A 2014 study found that training lowered resting HR through changes in the sinoatrial node itself (less HCN4), not through the nerves. What most limits applying this to human endurance athletes?

options.text: It was done in mice
options.why: Right: it is a mechanistic animal study. In humans the evidence comes from a few small drug-blockade studies.

options.text: It relied on self-reported training
options.why: Training was controlled by the researchers, and the node was studied directly.

options.text: It only observed retired athletes
options.why: It was an experiment comparing trained with sedentary animals, not an observational study.

options.text: It found no change in resting heart rate
options.why: It did: the trained animals had a lower resting HR, which persisted under blockade.
